title: Friction is not always a small inconvenience
objective: Given a service journey, identify learning, compliance and psychological costs, and distinguish simplification from changes to material access.
hook: Friction is not always a small inconvenience
story: Jo wants to book a repair but must print a form, find proof of purchase, and call during a short weekday window. The team describes the process as a few simple steps. Jo works those hours and has no printer. A reminder would leave those constraints in place.

concepts.title: Count the work from the participant’s side.

terms.Administrative burden: learning, compliance and psychological costs in an interaction with a service
terms.Learning cost: effort to find and understand what is required
terms.Compliance cost: time and resources needed to meet requirements

points: Administrative burden: learning, compliance and psychological costs in an interaction with a service
Learning cost: effort to find and understand what is required
Compliance cost: time and resources needed to meet requirements
concepts.text:
Administrative burden concerns costs experienced in an interaction. Learning cost includes finding a rule; compliance cost includes completing the required steps.

An instruction that looks brief to its author may require travel, documents and repeated calls. Map the journey from the participant’s position, including failed attempts. The number of screens alone does not measure the total burden.

concepts.title: The same process can impose unequal costs.

terms.Psychological cost: stress, stigma or loss of autonomy experienced in an interaction
terms.Distributional effect: differences in benefits or costs across people
terms.Accessibility: whether people with varied needs can use a service

points: Psychological cost: stress, stigma or loss of autonomy experienced in an interaction
Distributional effect: differences in benefits or costs across people
Accessibility: whether people with varied needs can use a service
concepts.text:
Psychological cost includes experiences such as stigma or an intrusive demand. Accessibility concerns whether different people can use the route. A distributional effect describes who carries the costs or receives the benefit.

Jo’s printer constraint differs from someone else’s language or mobility needs. Ask about relevant conditions without assuming that everyone in a demographic group has the same experience.

title: A reminder needs something feasible to remind
objective: Given a proposed reminder, distinguish an attention hypothesis from lack of access, and specify a meaningful test outcome.
hook: A reminder needs something feasible to remind
story: Visitors sometimes forget appointments after booking. Leo wants a bright message every day. Maya asks whether the time is clear, whether visitors can reschedule, and whether transport is reliable. Forgetting is one possible explanation; it is not the only reason an appointment is missed.

concepts.title: A message competes with other demands.

terms.Limited attention: finite capacity to notice and process information
terms.Salience: how much something stands out in a context
terms.Reminder: a cue intended to bring an action or intention to mind

points: Limited attention: finite capacity to notice and process information
Salience: how much something stands out in a context
Reminder: a cue intended to bring an action or intention to mind
concepts.text:
Limited attention means that relevant information may not come to mind when needed. Salience concerns what stands out; a reminder is a cue intended to bring an action back to mind.

A clear appointment time near the moment of planning may help. A brightly coloured message can also be noticed without making the visit feasible. Distinguish noticing from understanding and acting.

visual.caption: Failure at one hurdle does not establish failure at all the others.

concepts.title: Use the channel and moment that fit the action.

terms.Timing: when information is encountered relative to an action
terms.Actionable information: information that makes a next step clear
terms.Notification fatigue: reduced engagement associated with repeated or unwanted notifications

points: Timing: when information is encountered relative to an action
Actionable information: information that makes a next step clear
Notification fatigue: reduced engagement associated with repeated or unwanted notifications
concepts.text:
Timing matters because a cue can arrive before a person can act. Actionable information specifies the next step, including how to change a booking. Notification fatigue is a possible cost of repeated or unwanted messages.

A visitor may prefer one useful reminder with a rescheduling link over daily messages. Check preferences and access to the channel rather than assuming that more contact is better.

title: The way a choice is presented can matter
objective: Given a choice interface, identify a frame or default, distinguish presentation from a changed option, and protect informed choice.
hook: The way a choice is presented can matter
story: The café considers automatically renewing a membership. Leo expects the default to increase renewals. Maya asks whether people understand the charge and can leave easily. Another proposal describes the same repair contribution as either supporting a service or avoiding its loss. The team needs to examine both evidence and consent.

concepts.title: Equivalent descriptions can guide attention differently.

terms.Framing effect: a difference in judgment or choice associated with how a problem is described
terms.Reference point: a comparison standard used to evaluate an outcome
terms.Loss aversion: greater weight on losses than comparable gains in some models and settings

points: Framing effect: a difference in judgment or choice associated with how a problem is described
Reference point: a comparison standard used to evaluate an outcome
Loss aversion: greater weight on losses than comparable gains in some models and settings
concepts.text:
A framing effect concerns the description of a choice. A reference point supplies a comparison standard. Loss aversion describes a pattern in some models and settings; it is not a universal rule about every person.

Calling a membership change a gain or a loss can highlight different comparisons. Changing the actual price or eligibility is a different intervention from changing the description.

concepts.title: A default can have more than one explanation.

terms.Default option: the option applied if no active choice is made
terms.Status quo bias: a tendency to favour the existing state in some decisions
terms.Active choice: a requirement to select an option explicitly

points: Default option: the option applied if no active choice is made
Status quo bias: a tendency to favour the existing state in some decisions
Active choice: a requirement to select an option explicitly
concepts.text:
A default option applies when someone does not actively select otherwise. Status quo bias can contribute to staying with an existing state, but inattention, switching effort and perceived endorsement can also matter. Active choice asks for an explicit decision.

An automatic renewal could increase retention while leaving some people with an unwanted charge. Its uptake does not show that every retained member preferred it.

terms.Informed choice: a decision made with relevant understandable information
terms.Switching cost: effort or expense involved in changing an option
terms.Welfare: effects on people’s interests and wellbeing

points: Informed choice: a decision made with relevant understandable information
Switching cost: effort or expense involved in changing an option
Welfare: effects on people’s interests and wellbeing
concepts.text:
Informed choice needs understandable information. A switching cost can make an unwanted option hard to escape. Welfare concerns the consequences for people, not simply the service’s preferred uptake rate.

Show the price and renewal date clearly, offer an accessible cancellation route, and ask about unwanted charges. A default should not be treated as permission to hide information or manufacture agreement.

title: A future intention meets a present situation
objective: Given a missed intention, distinguish present bias from constraints and design a feasible, voluntary planning aid.
hook: A future intention meets a present situation
story: Sam plans to volunteer next month but postpones choosing a shift. The form takes time now, while the hoped-for benefit is later. Jo also postpones, but their employer has not released a work schedule. The same visible delay may have different causes.

concepts.title: Delay can reflect more than one process.

terms.Present bias: disproportionate weight on immediate costs or rewards relative to later ones
terms.Time inconsistency: a change in preferred plans as the time of a decision approaches

points: Present bias: disproportionate weight on immediate costs or rewards relative to later ones
Time inconsistency: a change in preferred plans as the time of a decision approaches
Constraint: a condition limiting feasible action
concepts.text:
Present bias concerns disproportionate emphasis on immediacy; time inconsistency concerns a change in preferred plans as a decision approaches. A constraint can instead make action genuinely unavailable.

Sam might value volunteering but avoid today’s form. Jo may be unable to select a shift without a work schedule. Observing delay alone cannot identify either person’s preferences or prove a self-control problem.

visual.title: Two possible reasons for delay
visual.caption: Similar delays do not establish identical causes.

concepts.title: A plan needs a usable cue and a feasible response.

terms.Implementation intention: an if-then plan linking a situation to a response
terms.Cue: a signal associated with an opportunity to act
terms.Feasibility: whether an action can be carried out under relevant conditions

points: Implementation intention: an if-then plan linking a situation to a response
Cue: a signal associated with an opportunity to act
Feasibility: whether an action can be carried out under relevant conditions
concepts.text:
An implementation intention links a cue to a response: if a situation occurs, then take a specified action. Feasibility still matters.

Sam might choose to book after receiving the next work schedule. That cue makes sense only if a suitable shift is available and the booking route works. An if-then sentence cannot supply transport, money or predictable working hours.

visual.title: A feasible if-then plan
items: Can I actually carry out this step?
visual.caption: A planning aid supports an intention; it does not remove every constraint.

concepts.title: Commitment can support a goal or impose a cost.

terms.Commitment device: an arrangement intended to make following a chosen plan more likely
terms.Voluntary participation: an informed choice without undue pressure
terms.Reversibility: the ability to change or leave an arrangement

points: Commitment device: an arrangement intended to make following a chosen plan more likely
Voluntary participation: an informed choice without undue pressure
Reversibility: the ability to change or leave an arrangement
concepts.text:
A commitment device changes the conditions around a future choice. Voluntary participation and reversibility matter because circumstances can change.

Sam may want a calendar booking and an easy way to reschedule. A large cancellation penalty could instead punish an unavoidable shift change. Evaluate the aid with the person’s interests in view, including who bears the risk of an unexpected problem.

visual.title: Review a planning aid
items: What could make the plan infeasible?
Can the arrangement be revised fairly?
visual.caption: Support for follow-through should not become punishment for uncertainty.

evidence:
Present-biased models explain some patterns of changing choice; they do not diagnose a person from a missed task. Research on implementation intentions examines specified plans, tasks and populations, with effects that depend on those conditions.

A planning aid needs an existing goal, a feasible response and an acceptable burden. It cannot substitute for material resources or predictable access.

Ask each person what prevents booking and whether a feasible shift can currently be chosen.

feedback: The same delay can arise from different processes and constraints.
This can distinguish immediate effort, missing information and other barriers.

An optional cue to check availability after the schedule arrives, with a straightforward rescheduling route.

title: A social norm message needs a truthful comparison
objective: Given a norm message, distinguish descriptive and injunctive claims, identify the relevant comparison group, and assess a possible boomerang effect.
hook: A social norm message needs a truthful comparison

concepts.title: What people do and what they approve are different.

points: Descriptive norm: a perception of what people commonly do in a relevant group

terms.Boomerang effect: a change opposite to the intended direction
terms.Heterogeneous effect: an effect that differs across people or settings
terms.Baseline behaviour: behaviour measured before a proposed change

points: Boomerang effect: a change opposite to the intended direction

title: An incentive can change more than the payoff
objective: Given an incentive proposal, identify the rewarded measure, possible substitution and distributional costs, and specify outcomes beyond the rewarded count.
hook: An incentive can change more than the payoff
story: The café proposes rewarding volunteers for the number of repairs completed. Sam worries that difficult cases will be avoided and repair quality may fall. Jo says modest reimbursement for travel would solve a different problem. The team needs to distinguish removing a cost from paying for a target count.

concepts.title: Ask exactly what the arrangement rewards.

terms.Incentive: a consequence that changes the relative attractiveness of actions
terms.Opportunity cost: the value of an alternative forgone

points: Incentive: a consequence that changes the relative attractiveness of actions
Reimbursement: repayment of a cost incurred
Opportunity cost: the value of an alternative forgone
concepts.text:
An incentive changes the relative attractiveness of actions. Reimbursement repays a cost; opportunity cost concerns the alternative a person gives up. These can overlap in practice but answer different questions.

Travel reimbursement may make a shift affordable. A payment for repair count rewards a particular result. Neither proposal should be evaluated by a general claim that money either solves motivation or damages it.

visual.title: Two proposals with different purposes
right: Effort may shift toward that result
visual.caption: Identify the purpose and likely costs before choosing an evaluation.

concepts.title: The rewarded measure can displace the intended outcome.

terms.Proxy measure: an indirect indicator used for something that matters
terms.Substitution effect: a shift toward an action made relatively more attractive
terms.Gaming: improving a measured result without the intended underlying benefit

points: Proxy measure: an indirect indicator used for something that matters
Substitution effect: a shift toward an action made relatively more attractive
Gaming: improving a measured result without the intended underlying benefit
concepts.text:
A proxy measure stands in for something harder to observe. A substitution effect can shift activity toward the rewarded action. Gaming improves the measured result without the intended benefit.

Counting completed repairs may encourage quick cases, or change how a completion is recorded. Measure quality, difficult-case access and unintended costs alongside throughput. Not every rise in the count is gaming, so investigate rather than presume misconduct.

visual.title: Follow the incentive beyond the count
items: More effort or different case selection
visual.caption: The figure shows competing hypotheses, not a claim about volunteers’ motives.

concepts.title: Meaning and fairness can affect a response.

terms.Motivational crowding: a change in other motivation associated with an external intervention
terms.Acceptability: whether an arrangement is considered appropriate by affected people
terms.Distribution: how benefits and burdens are shared

points: Motivational crowding: a change in other motivation associated with an external intervention
Acceptability: whether an arrangement is considered appropriate by affected people
Distribution: how benefits and burdens are shared
concepts.text:
Motivational crowding describes a possible change in other motivation. Acceptability concerns how people judge an arrangement, while distribution concerns who gains and who pays its costs.

A payment can communicate recognition, control or a commercial expectation depending on the setting. Ask affected people, compare meaningful outcomes, and examine who can meet the rewarded target. Do not turn a possible crowding effect into a rule against paying people fairly.

items: Who can participate and who bears costs?
visual.caption: Fair compensation and a poorly designed performance target are different questions.

evidence:
Research reviews describe varied incentive effects across tasks, populations and arrangements. Effects on other motivation are possible, but they do not justify the blanket claim that payments backfire or that unpaid participation is preferable.

Evaluate the specified arrangement over an appropriate period. Preserve fair compensation and examine quality, access, costs and effects beyond the rewarded measure.

title: A useful result still needs an ethical decision
objective: Given a positive evaluation, judge whether to adapt, expand, investigate or stop using evidence on benefit, distribution, autonomy, implementation and uncertainty.
hook: A useful result still needs an ethical decision
story: A booking pilot increases attendance on average. Some visitors report unwanted messages; people without reliable internet still struggle. concepts.title: An average can hide different consequences.

terms.Average treatment effect: an average difference attributable to an intervention in a defined population under the study conditions
terms.Equity: attention to the fairness of opportunities, benefits and burdens
terms.Opportunity cost: the value of an alternative forgone

points: Average treatment effect: an average difference attributable to an intervention in a defined population under the study conditions
Equity: attention to the fairness of opportunities, benefits and burdens
Opportunity cost: the value of an alternative forgone
concepts.text:
An average treatment effect summarizes a defined comparison, not a benefit for every person. Equity asks about fair opportunities and distribution. Opportunity cost concerns what another use of the resources could achieve.

An attendance gain could coexist with unwanted contacts or exclusion of people needing a phone route. Examine these consequences and compare feasible alternatives, including a service-capacity change. A dashboard average cannot make the value judgment on its own.
